The circle is the most fundamental and symmetric of all geometric curves. It's defined as the set of all points in a plane equidistant from a fixed point called the center. The equation in Cartesian coordinates is x minus h squared plus y minus k squared equals r squared, where h and k give the center and r is the radius. In polar coordinates, it's simply r equals c. The circumference is two pi r, and the area is pi r squared—a formula that Archimedes first proved rigorously using the method of exhaustion. Pi itself, approximately three point one four one five nine, is defined as the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, and it's a transcendental number. A circle is actually a degenerate case of an ellipse—it appears when the two foci of an ellipse coincide at the center, giving an eccentricity of exactly zero. If you cut a right circular cone with a plane parallel to its base, you get a circle. Thales's theorem tells us that if three points A, B, and C lie on a circle where the line from A to C is a diameter, then the angle at B is a right angle. Ptolemy's theorem applies to cyclic quadrilaterals, those inscribed in a circle—the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides. Apollonian circles are defined as the set of points whose distances to two fixed points are in a constant ratio. When that ratio is one, the locus is a circle. The circle also serves as a generating curve for other shapes. Roll a circle along a flat line and you trace out a cycloid. Roll a circle of one radius around the outside of another circle of equal radius and you trace out a cardioid. The circle represents the ultimate symbol of symmetry and infinity in mathematics—the transition from discrete polygons to continuous curves. Its properties guided the astronomical models of Ptolemy and Copernicus, who relied on circular epicycles to explain planetary motions. The ancient Greek quest to square the circle—to construct a square with the same area as a given circle using only compass and straightedge—remained unsolved for over two thousand years until Ferdinand von Lindemann proved it impossible in eighteen eighty-two.
